# Your Environment {#chp:env}

Code runs somewhere: on some operating system, with some packages installed,
some options set, and some environment variables defined. This chapter helps
you read that environment and change it temporarily without leaving a mess.

## Attach several packages at once {#sec:pkg-attach}

`pkg_attach()` is a vectorized `library()`. `pkg_attach2()` goes a step further
and installs packages that are missing first:

```{r}
pkg_attach("stats", "utils")  # equivalent to two library() calls
```

```r
pkg_attach2("ggplot2", "dplyr")  # installs any that are missing, then attaches
```

## Test whether a package is available {#sec:loadable}

`loadable()` is a concise alternative to `requireNamespace(quietly = TRUE)`.
It is useful for optional dependencies:

```{r}
loadable("stats")
loadable("nonexistent.package.xyz")
```

## Let an option fall back to an environment variable {#sec:env-option}

Package authors often want users to configure behavior either with
`options()` in `.Rprofile`, or with an environment variable in `.Renviron`.
`env_option()` checks `options()` first, then looks for an environment variable
named `R_<NAME>` (uppercased, dots turned into underscores):

```{r}
Sys.setenv(R_XFUN_TEST_OPTION = "from-env")
env_option("xfun.test.option")     # "from-env"

options(xfun.test.option = TRUE)
env_option("xfun.test.option")     # TRUE: options() wins
options(xfun.test.option = NULL)   # reset
env_option("xfun.test.option")     # "from-env" again
Sys.unsetenv("R_XFUN_TEST_OPTION")
```

## Set an environment variable for a while {#sec:set-envvar}

`set_envvar()` sets variables and returns their previous values, so you can put
things back when you are done:

```{r}
old = set_envvar(c(MY_TOKEN = "secret"))
Sys.getenv("MY_TOKEN")
set_envvar(old)  # restore
Sys.getenv("MY_TOKEN")
```

## Know which OS you are on {#sec:os}

The `is_*()` family tells you the current operating system, without parsing
`R.version` yourself:

```{r}
is_windows()
is_macos()
is_linux()
is_unix()   # TRUE on macOS and Linux
is_arm64()  # TRUE on Apple silicon
```

## Get a compact session summary {#sec:session-info}

When you report a bug, you want session info that is short and focused.
`session_info()` trims `sessionInfo()`: no base-package noise, no BLAS details.
Give it a list of packages for a focused summary:

```{r}
session_info(c("xfun", "litedown"), dependencies = FALSE)
```

## Do something only once {#sec:do-once}

A deprecation message that prints on every call is annoying. `do_once()` runs
a task the first time and skips it afterward in the same R session:

```{r}
for (i in 1:3) {
  do_once(message("This prints once."), "my-one-time-task")
}
```

## List the base R packages {#sec:base-pkgs}

Sometimes you need to tell the packages that ship with R from the ones people
installed. `base_pkgs()` returns the names of the base packages:

```{r}
base_pkgs()
setdiff(c("stats", "xfun"), base_pkgs())  # keep only the non-base ones
```

## Require a minimal package version {#sec:pkg-available}

`loadable()` says whether a package can be loaded. `pkg_available()` also checks
the version, which is handy when your code needs a feature from a recent
release:

```{r}
pkg_available("stats")
pkg_available("stats", "99.0")          # too new
pkg_available("nonexistent.package.xyz")
```

## Load packages without attaching them {#sec:pkg-load}

`pkg_load()` is a vectorized `requireNamespace()`: it loads packages but does
not put them on the search path. It returns (invisibly) a logical vector, and
signals an error if any package is missing. Set `error = FALSE` to get the
vector without the error:

```{r}
pkg_load("stats", "utils")
ok = pkg_load("stats", "nonexistent.package.xyz", error = FALSE)
ok
```

## Install missing packages while loading {#sec:pkg-load2}

`pkg_load2()` is `pkg_load(install = TRUE)`: whatever is missing gets installed
first with `install.packages()`. Set a CRAN mirror in `options(repos = )` before
you rely on this:

```r
pkg_load2("jsonlite", "yaml")  # install if needed, load without attaching
```

## Detect `R CMD check` and CRAN incoming checks {#sec:is-check}

Tests and examples sometimes need to behave differently under `R CMD check`
(skip slow or network-bound code, for example). `is_R_CMD_check()` tells you
whether you are inside a check, and `is_CRAN_incoming()` whether it is the
extra check CRAN runs on submissions:

```{r}
is_R_CMD_check()
is_CRAN_incoming()
```

Both are `FALSE` in an ordinary session. Under a check, `is_R_CMD_check()`
returns `TRUE`, so a typical use is `if (!is_R_CMD_check()) { ...slow code... }`.
